Photographer Tyler Stalman is back with his annual iPhone camera review. Here's his take on the iPhone 18 Pro's new variable aperture, Photographic Styles, Apple Reference Image, and more.

Stalman dives into iPhone 18 Pro camera's variable aperture

While this year's iPhone 18 Pro brings several new features including the 2nm A20 Pro chip, new vapor chamber, and smaller Dynamic Island, the biggest camera upgrade is arguably the new variable aperture system.

Also new this year are updates to Cinematic mode, new Photographic Styles with new texture controls, Apple Reference Image, and further refinements to pro controls in the Camera app.

Today, photographer Tyler Stalman released a comprehensive video review of the new iPhone 18 Pro's hardware and software features, adding to the wave of reviews that have come out as the embargo has lifted, our own review included.

Stalman notes that while he loved last year's iPhone 17 Pro's Cosmic Orange color, it tends to show up in reflections when shooting through glass. For this reason, he thinks pro photographers will likely gravitate toward the Burgundy or Black, since those two colors are less likely to cast unwanted color onto photos or videos.

He also mentions up top that this review compares the iPhone 18 Pro's camera to the iPhone 15 Pro's, while the video itself is shot almost entirely on the iPhone 17 Pro.

Moving on to the main camera upgrade, which is the new variable aperture, Stalman says its inclusion is "a step toward (the iPhone) being a real camera."

He also points out that the wider f/1.48 aperture lets more light hit the sensor, which helps keep ISO lower in low-light situations and rely less on Night mode.

This section of the review includes some excellent photos of the aperture blades opening and closing, with Stalman noting that Apple's design is rather unique, with the aperture blades sitting above the main lens element rather than being deeper inside the lens like a traditional camera lens.

Stalman also notes that the iPhone 18 Pro's 4x zoom (also seen on last year's iPhone) is an improvement over the iPhone 16 Pro's 5x zoom, since the 5x zoom can sometimes feel a touch too tight.

Going too far, he briefly mentions the new AI editing tools like Clean Up, Extend, and Reframe, noting that while these tools are technically impressive and realistic, they can make changes so large that the final image doesn't quite feel like the original photo anymore.

Moving on to the iPhone 18 Pro's new texture options, including Soft Skin, Glow, and Film, Stalman walks through each one from 0 to 100 strength. As for his impressions, he finds that Soft Skin subtly reduces skin detail rather than simply blurring it, while Glow adds a spread of highlights similar to a black mist filter.

He's also impressed by the grain and halation of the Film effect, though he wishes Apple offered more control over the amount of grain.

The review also touches on Apple Reference Image, Cinematic mode on iPhone (with Stalman still recommending Apple Log for truly cinematic video), the new Apple Log 2, and naturally includes photo and video comparisons between the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro.
